summary: Specifies a JMAP data model for synchronizing email with a server. Clients can search, access, organize, and send messages and get push notifications for quick resynchronization. It builds on RFC 8620 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: JMAP is a way for apps to fetch and change data over the network using JSON. This document defines what mail looks like in JMAP: folders, conversations, individual messages, and the operations that read and change them.

questions: how does jmap differ from imap
how do i send email with jmap
subtitle: How a mail app reads, searches, organises and sends email over JMAP, with one JSON data model instead of IMAP and SMTP plumbing.

tldr.problem: Mail clients need an efficient and consistent way to synchronise, search, organise and send email, without each one parsing MIME and character encodings for itself.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8621 defines Mailbox, Thread, Email, SearchSnippet, Identity, EmailSubmission and VacationResponse data types for the JMAP protocol, together with the methods that read and change them.
tldr.outcome: A client can fetch a parsed, simplified view of each message, query across mailboxes and threads, and send mail through the same API. It is a Proposed Standard that builds on RFC 8620.

today: RFC 8621 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2019. It updates RFC 5788, the IMAP keyword registry, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What JMAP for Mail Defines
sections.content:
The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) (RFC 8620) is a generic protocol for synchronising data, such as mail, calendars, or contacts, between a client and a server. It is optimised for mobile and web environments and aims to provide a consistent interface to different data types. RFC 8621 defines a data model for accessing a mail store over JMAP, allowing a client to query, read, organise and submit mail for sending.

The data model is designed to allow a server to provide consistent access to the same data via IMAP (RFC 3501) as well as JMAP. As in IMAP, a message must belong to a mailbox, but in JMAP its id does not change if it moves between mailboxes, and the server may allow it to belong to multiple mailboxes simultaneously, which a user agent often shows as labels rather than folders.

As in IMAP, messages may also be assigned zero or more keywords: short arbitrary strings, primarily intended to store metadata to inform client display, such as unread status or whether a message has been replied to. An IANA registry allows common semantics to be shared between clients and extended easily in the future. A message and its replies are linked on the server by a common Thread id, so a client may fetch the list of messages with a particular Thread id to present a threaded or conversational interface. Permissions for message access happen on a per-mailbox basis, and a server may give the user restricted permissions for certain mailboxes, for example when another user's inbox has been shared read-only with them.
sections.plainLanguage: JMAP is a way for apps to fetch and change data over the network using JSON. This document defines what mail looks like in JMAP: folders, conversations, individual messages, and the operations that read and change them.

sections.title: Capabilities and Push Notifications
sections.content:
The document defines three capability URIs, added to the capabilities object that the JMAP Session object returns. urn:ietf:params:jmap:mail represents support for the Mailbox, Thread, Email and SearchSnippet data types and their methods, and its value in the session capabilities property is an empty object. urn:ietf:params:jmap:submission represents support for the Identity and EmailSubmission data types, and urn:ietf:params:jmap:vacationresponse represents support for the VacationResponse data type, whose value is an empty object in both the session capabilities and the account capabilities.

Each account's accountCapabilities property carries the server's capabilities and permissions for that account. For the mail capability these are maxMailboxesPerEmail, the maximum number of mailboxes one Email can be assigned to; maxMailboxDepth, the maximum depth of the mailbox hierarchy; maxSizeMailboxName, the maximum length in octets of a mailbox name, which MUST be at least 100; maxSizeAttachmentsPerEmail, the maximum total size of unencoded attachments; emailQuerySortOptions, the list of sort properties the server supports; and mayCreateTopLevelMailbox. For the submission capability they are maxDelayedSend, the number of seconds of delayed sending the server supports, which is 0 if it does not support it, and submissionExtensions, the set of SMTP submission extensions the server supports.

The server MUST include the appropriate capability strings in the accountCapabilities of any account with which the user may use those data types, and the supported data types may differ between accounts. A user may have all three sets of data in a personal account and only mail data in a shared account, where they cannot send as that account and cannot view or set its vacation response.

Servers MUST support the JMAP push mechanism so that clients receive notifications when the state changes for any of these types. Servers implementing the mail capability MUST also support pushing state changes for a type called EmailDelivery, which exists only as part of the push mechanism and has no methods. Its state string MUST change whenever a new Email is added to the store, and SHOULD NOT change on any other change to the Email objects, for example when one is marked as read or deleted. A client in a battery-constrained environment can register for pushes for the EmailDelivery type rather than the Email type, so that it fetches new mail immediately but delays changes the user initiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The server advertises, per account, which of these features it supports and what its limits are, such as the longest mailbox name it accepts. It also pushes a notification when something changes, and there is a special notification type that fires only when new mail arrives, so a phone can show an alert without fetching everything else.

sections.title: Mailboxes, Threads and Keywords
sections.content:
A Mailbox represents a named set of Email objects and is the primary mechanism for organising messages within an account, analogous to a folder or a label in other systems. For compatibility with IMAP, an Email MUST belong to one or more Mailboxes, and the Email id does not change when the Email changes Mailboxes.

A Mailbox object has an immutable server-set id; a user-visible name, which MUST be a Net-Unicode string of at least one character, with no two sibling mailboxes having both the same parent and the same name; a parentId that is null at the top level, with mailboxes forming acyclic forests and no loops; and a role that identifies mailboxes with a particular common purpose, such as the inbox, regardless of the localised name. The role value is shared with IMAP through the SPECIAL-USE extension, but unlike in IMAP, a Mailbox MUST only have a single role, and there MUST NOT be two mailboxes in the same account with the same role. A Mailbox also has a sortOrder for display, and four server-set counters: totalEmails, unreadEmails, totalThreads and unreadThreads. Unread means an Email that has neither the $seen nor the $draft keyword, and the trash mailbox is treated separately so that emails only in the trash do not affect the unread thread count of other mailboxes.

Each Mailbox also carries myRights, the set of rights the user has over it, which are backwards compatible with IMAP ACLs (RFC 4314): mayReadItems, mayAddItems, mayRemoveItems and maySetSeen. Permissions for message access therefore happen on a per-mailbox basis.

A message and its replies are linked on the server by a common Thread id, and clients may fetch the list of messages with a particular Thread id to present a threaded or conversational interface. Threads have their own get and changes methods.
sections.plainLanguage: Mailboxes are the folders, and they can be nested. A message keeps the same id when it moves between folders, and it can sit in several folders at once, which many apps show as labels. Each folder also carries counts, such as how many unread messages and unread conversations it holds, and the rights the user has over it.

sections.title: The Email Object
sections.content:
An Email object is a representation of a message (RFC 5322), which allows clients to avoid the complexities of MIME parsing, transfer encoding and character encoding. Broadly, a message consists of a list of header fields and then a body, and the Email type lets a client take the full structure or use simplified properties.

The metadata properties are not derived from parsing the message itself: id, which is the JMAP object id and not the Message-ID header value; blobId, which identifies the raw octets of the message; threadId, the Thread the message belongs to; mailboxIds, the set of mailboxes it belongs to; keywords; size, the number of octets in the raw data; and receivedAt, the date the message was received by the store, which is the internal date in IMAP.

Keywords are shared with IMAP. Six system keywords come from IMAP, and four of them have their first character changed from a backslash to a dollar sign in JMAP and carry a particular meaning: $draft, the message is a draft the user is composing; $seen, the message has been read; $flagged, the message has been flagged for urgent or special attention; and $answered, the message has been replied to. The IMAP \Recent keyword is not exposed over JMAP, and the IMAP \Deleted keyword is also not present, because IMAP uses a delete-and-expunge model that JMAP does not. Any message with the \Deleted keyword MUST NOT be visible via JMAP, and is not counted in the Mailbox counters. Users may add arbitrary keywords, which are case-insensitive strings of 1 to 255 characters in the ASCII subset, and because JSON is case sensitive servers MUST return keywords in lowercase. The IANA registry assigns meaning to some other keywords, including $forwarded, $phishing, $junk and $notjunk.

Header field properties are derived from the message header fields. All header fields may be fetched in a raw form, and some also in a parsed form; the vast majority of clients should use an appropriate parsed form, so they avoid the complexities of the encodings a valid message may use.

The body of a message is normally a MIME-encoded set of documents in a tree, but most clients present a flat model of a body with a set of attachments, and flattening causes inconsistency between clients. So, besides bodyStructure, which gives the full tree, the Email object contains three flat lists: textBody and htmlBody, which hold the parts to render sequentially as the body of the message, preferring a plaintext or an HTML representation respectively, and attachments, which holds the parts to present as attachments. The bodyValues property lets a client fetch the value of text parts directly, with the server decoding the charset into unicode, and it is a separate property to avoid duplicating large amounts of data when a client fetches more than one of bodyStructure, textBody and htmlBody.
sections.plainLanguage: The Email object is the parsed view of one message. It gives the client the sender, subject, date, size, which folders it is in and its flags, with the header fields already decoded into forms a program can use. The body is offered both as the full MIME tree and as flat lists of text, HTML and attachments, so the client can choose how much detail it wants.

sections.title: Searching, Sorting and Collapsing
sections.content:
Email/query is the standard JMAP query method with one extra argument, collapseThreads. If it is true, Emails in the same Thread as a previous Email in the list, given the filter and sort order, are removed from the list, so at most one Email per Thread is included. In quality implementations the total is fast to calculate when the filter consists solely of a single inMailbox property, since it is the same as the corresponding Mailbox counter.

A FilterCondition has properties any of which may be omitted: inMailbox and inMailboxOtherThan; before and after on the receivedAt date; minSize and maxSize; allInThreadHaveKeyword, someInThreadHaveKeyword and noneInThreadHaveKeyword; hasKeyword and notKeyword; hasAttachment; and text searches over from, to, cc, bcc, subject, body, and a header named by a one or two element array. If zero properties are specified the condition always evaluates to true, and if multiple properties are specified all must apply. The exact semantics for matching strings are deliberately not defined, to allow flexibility in indexing, but text SHOULD be matched case-insensitively, text in single or double quotes SHOULD be treated as a phrase search, and when searching inside a text/html body part any text considered markup rather than content SHOULD be ignored, while presentation attributes such as alt and title SHOULD still be considered.

For sorting, receivedAt MUST be supported, and size, from, to, subject, sentAt, hasKeyword, allInThreadHaveKeyword and someInThreadHaveKeyword SHOULD be supported. A client can discover which properties the server supports by inspecting the account's capabilities object.

Email/set is the standard set method and encompasses creating a draft, changing the keywords of an Email, adding or removing an Email to or from mailboxes, and deleting Emails. The document also defines Email/copy, Email/import, Email/parse and Email/queryChanges. Mailbox, Thread, Email and SearchSnippet each have their own get, changes, query or queryChanges methods.

A SearchSnippet holds the part of a message that matched a search. It has the Email id it applies to, the subject with the matching words wrapped in mark tags, and a preview of the relevant section of the body, converted to plaintext if it was originally HTML. The preview MUST NOT be bigger than 255 octets, and if the server cannot determine snippets it MUST return null for both the subject and the preview.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for messages by describing what it wants, such as a folder, a date range, a size, a flag, or words in the text. The server returns matching messages in the order asked for. One option collapses each conversation down to a single message, which is what a phone app usually wants.

sections.title: Identities, Sending Mail and Vacation Replies
sections.content:
An Identity stores information about an email address or domain the user may send from: the From name the client SHOULD use, the From email address the client MUST use, a reply-to address, a bcc address, and text and HTML signatures to insert into new messages. If the mailbox part of the address is the single character asterisk, the client may use any valid address ending in that domain. Several identities may share the same email address, so the user can choose between different names and signatures.

An EmailSubmission object represents the submission of an Email for delivery to one or more recipients. It holds the Identity to associate with the submission, the Email to send, which does not have to be a draft, and an envelope with the mailFrom address and the rcptTo addresses, including any parameters for the SMTP commands. If the envelope is null or omitted on creation, the server generates it: mailFrom from the Sender header field if present, otherwise from the From header field, taking the first address in the last such header field, and using the Identity's address instead if the found address is not allowed by that Identity; rcptTo from the deduplicated set of addresses in the To, Cc and Bcc header fields. The server sets sendAt to the time the message will be released for delivery if the client successfully used FUTURERELEASE (RFC 4865), and otherwise to the time the submission was created.

The undoStatus property says whether the submission may be canceled, and is one of pending, meaning it may be possible to cancel it, final, meaning the message has been relayed to at least one recipient in a manner that cannot be recalled, and canceled. A client can attempt to cancel a pending submission by setting this property to canceled. The deliveryStatus maps each recipient address to a DeliveryStatus object with the SMTP reply the server last got, and may not be supported by all servers.

A VacationResponse object holds the automatic reply settings for an account. There MUST be exactly one per account and its id is singleton. It has isEnabled, fromDate and toDate, which may be null for immediate effect or no end date, a subject, and a textBody and htmlBody, either of which may be null, in which case the server generates one from the other. The RFC reminds implementors to follow the recommendations of RFC 3834, because automated message sending can otherwise produce undesirable behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending is also part of the same API. The client picks an identity, the server works out the envelope from the message headers, and the client can often cancel the message before it goes out. An out-of-office setting is a single object with the dates and the text of the reply.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations of JMAP (RFC 8620) apply, and the document adds considerations specific to the new data types.

Service providers typically perform security filtering on incoming messages, so the detection of content type and charset for the security filter should align with the heuristics the JMAP server uses. Servers that apply such heuristics SHOULD document them and provide a mechanism to turn them off when they are misaligned with the security filter used at a particular mail host. Automatic conversion of charsets that allow hidden channels for ASCII text, such as UTF-7, has been problematic for security filters, so implementations can mitigate this by having such conversions off by default and separately configurable. A client may request a maximum length for a textual body part, but truncating the data may change its semantic meaning, for example by changing the location of a URL, so servers that scan for links to malicious sites should either ensure the truncation is not at a semantically significant point or rescan the truncated value.

HTML message bodies give richer formatting but raise a number of security challenges, especially in a webmail context combined with interface HTML. The document lists them: embedded JavaScript can rewrite the message to change its content on subsequent opening, and in webmail systems, if it runs in the same origin as the interface, it can access and exfiltrate all private data accessible to the user, and can rewrite the interface to undetectably phish passwords. HTML documents may load content directly from the Internet, for example an img tag with an external source, which may leak to the sender that a message was opened along with the recipient's IP address, and cookies may be sent and set, allowing tracking between different messages. CSS can break the layout or create phishing vulnerabilities, and in a webmail context styles from a message can apply to interface elements. The link text in HTML has no necessary correlation with the actual target, which makes phishing more convincing. Links opened from a message may leak private information in the Referer header. Forms can mimic login boxes.

Mitigations include filtering HTML before rendering with a well-tested library and a carefully vetted whitelist-only approach rather than a blacklist, and using the same parser for filtering that the HTML rendering engine uses. The document also covers displaying multiple parts, email submission, partial account access and permission to send from an address.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is HTML mail. It can run scripts, load pictures from the internet, and imitate the login box of the webmail page itself. The document tells client writers to strip it carefully and to keep the account limits in mind.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: Three JMAP capabilities are registered, for mail, submission and vacationresponse. The IMAP and JMAP Keywords registry, established by RFC 5788, gains registrations for the JMAP keywords $draft, $seen, $flagged and $answered, and a registration for the $recent keyword. The IMAP Mailbox Name Attributes registry gains the inbox role. A JMAP Error Codes registry is created, with entries including mailboxHasChild, mailboxHasEmail, blobNotFound, tooManyKeywords, tooManyMailboxes, invalidEmail, tooManyRecipients, noRecipients, invalidRecipients, forbiddenMailFrom, forbiddenFrom and forbiddenToSend.
sections.plainLanguage: The official lists get new entries: three capabilities, the standard keywords, the inbox role and a set of error codes for the mail API.

viz.caption: THE RISKS OF HTML MAIL (RFC 8621, SECTION 9.2)

items.title: Embedded JavaScript
items.text: Can rewrite the message so it changes on later openings, and in webmail can read and send out the user's other data.

items.title: Remote content
items.text: An img tag with an external source tells the sender that the message was opened and reveals the recipient's IP address.

items.title: Cookies
items.text: Cookies set by a message can track the user between different messages and between websites.

items.title: CSS
items.text: Can break the layout, draw outside the message, or change how the webmail interface looks.

items.title: Link text
items.text: The text of a link need not match where it goes, which makes phishing more convincing.

items.title: Forms
items.text: A form in a message can imitate a login box and post what the user types to the attacker.
